title: Query Executor
overview:
In this final project you will implement three new **physical operators** for the query execution engine: **SortExec**, **AggregateExec**, and **IndexScanExec**.

All operators follow the **Volcano iterator model**: each operator implements `Open()`, `Next()`, and `Close()`. `Open()` initializes state, `Next()` returns one row at a time (or `nullopt` at end of stream), and `Close()` releases resources. The execution engine calls the top-level operator's `Next()` repeatedly to pull results through the operator tree.

**Operator tree example:**
```
ProjectExec
  └── SortExec(age DESC)
        └── AggregateExec(GROUP BY dept, SUM(salary))
              └── SeqScanExec(employees)
```

Each `Next()` call at the top cascades down through the tree. Sort and Aggregate are **blocking operators** — they must consume all input from their child before producing any output.

tasks.title: Sort Executor
tasks.description: The `SortExec` sorts all rows from its child according to one or more sort keys, each with an ascending/descending direction.

functions.name: Open()
functions.description:
Pull all rows from the child executor into `sorted_rows_`. Sort them using `std::sort` with a custom comparator that iterates through `sort_keys_`, comparing values from each row. For ascending keys, use `<`; for descending, use `>`.

This is a **blocking operation** — all input must be materialized before any output can be produced.
hints: Call `child_->Open()` first.
Loop: `while (auto row = child_->Next()) sorted_rows_.push_back(*row);`
Comparator lambda: for each sort key, extract `row[key.column_name]` from both rows. If they differ, return the comparison result. If equal, move to the next key.
Reset `idx_ = 0` for the Next() cursor.

functions.name: Next() → optional<Row>
functions.description: Return the next row from the sorted result, or `nullopt` if exhausted.
hints: Return `sorted_rows_[idx_++]` if `idx_ < sorted_rows_.size()`.

tasks.title: Aggregate Executor
tasks.description:
The `AggregateExec` groups rows by zero or more group-by columns and computes aggregate functions for each group using a **hash-based** strategy.

Each `AggregateSpec` describes one aggregate computation:
- `func`: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, or MAX
- `column_name`: the column to aggregate (empty for COUNT(*))
- `output_name`: the key in the result row (e.g., "SUM(salary)")
- `is_count_star`: true for COUNT(*)

functions.name: Open()
functions.description:
Pull all rows from the child. For each row, build a **group key** string from the group-by column values (e.g., `"sales|"` for dept=sales). Maintain a hash map from group key to accumulator state.

**Accumulator state per aggregate:**
- COUNT: increment a counter
- SUM: add the numeric value
- AVG: track sum and count, divide at the end
- MIN/MAX: track the current extreme value

After processing all input, build result rows — one per group — containing group column values plus aggregate results. Store in `result_rows_`.

**Special case:** If there are no group-by columns, there is exactly one result row (even on empty input — COUNT returns 0).
hints: Use `unordered_map<string, pair<Row, vector<AccState>>>` where AccState tracks sum/count/min/max per aggregate.
Group key: concatenate `row[col].ToString() + "|"` for each group-by column.
For SUM/AVG, convert INTEGER values to double before accumulating.
For MIN/MAX, compare using `Value::operator<` and `Value::operator>`.
The first row in each group provides the template for group column values.

functions.name: Next() → optional<Row>
functions.description: Return the next group's aggregated result from `result_rows_`, or `nullopt` if exhausted.
hints: Same pattern as SortExec::Next().

tasks.title: Index Scan Executor
tasks.description: The `IndexScanExec` uses a B+-Tree index to efficiently retrieve records within a key range, instead of scanning the entire table.

functions.name: Open()
functions.description: Call `index_->RangeScan(begin_key_, end_key_)` to get all matching `(key, page_id)` pairs. Store in `results_` and reset the cursor.
hints: One line: `results_ = index_->RangeScan(begin_key_, end_key_);`
Reset `idx_ = 0`.

functions.name: Next() → optional<Row>
functions.description: Get the next `(key, page_id)` from `results_`. Use the ObjectManager to fetch the record bytes from that page (slot 0), deserialize them into a Row, and return it.
hints: If `idx_ >= results_.size()`, return `nullopt`.
`auto [key, pid] = results_[idx_++];`
Fetch bytes: `object_manager_->GetRecord(pid, 0)`.
Deserialize: `ObjectManager::DeserializeRow(bytes, schema_)`.

breakdown.covers: Integer ASC/DESC, string sort, multi-key, empty input
COUNT(*), SUM, GROUP BY (single/multiple groups), AVG/MIN/MAX, empty input
Point lookup, range scan, empty range

testing.note: Sort and Aggregate tests use a `MockExecutor` (provided in executor.h) for isolation. IndexScan tests set up a real B+-Tree with disk-backed records. Project #1-#4 reference implementations are provided.
testing.platforms: macOS or Linux, on either Intel or ARM. On Windows, build inside WSL: a native Windows toolchain is refused, because the reference libraries these downloads carry are built for macOS and Linux only.

hints: Start with SortExec — it's the simplest (materialize + std::sort + iterate).
For AggregateExec, get COUNT(*) working first (no column needed), then add SUM, then the rest.
The AVG aggregate requires tracking both sum and count separately, then dividing in the result-building phase.
IndexScanExec is short (~15 lines total) but depends on the B+-Tree and ObjectManager being correct — both come from the reference library in this download, so they already are.
All three executors follow the same Volcano pattern: Open() does the heavy work, Next() returns one result at a time.
Look at the existing `FilterExec` and `HashJoinExec` in `src/execution/` as examples of the Volcano pattern.
The `MockExecutor` in `executor.h` lets you test your operators in isolation without needing real tables.

submission.where: Upload the archive to PLMS (https://plms.postech.ac.kr) under Project #5 before the deadline. Submissions sent by email, or left anywhere else, are not collected.
submission.note: Keep the original directory layout inside the archive (src/…), so the files drop straight back into the project tree. Submit only the files you edited: no build/ directory, no compiled objects, no reference libraries.

report.description: What each function you write has to solve, and what the given code it calls does for it. Only what your functions actually use — not every header in the download. The earlier projects are out of scope: they arrive as a compiled library.
The algorithm you chose for each function, and why that one.
Which part of the design is which part of your code, by file and line.
The argument that your code is right.

blocks.text: **For each module below, write one expression that is always true of it** — true before any of its functions is called, and true again every time one of them returns. It may go false in the middle of a function; that is what makes it worth writing down.
The expression is symbols, not words:
If something is hard to put in symbols, define it as a variable in words, then use the variable in the expression:

code: P = the spaces with a car in them
F = the spaces that are empty
for i in 0 .. total_spaces-1:  i in P or i in F

blocks.text: A module holds several such expressions true at once. Pick one and get it right; you do not have to find them all.
**For each function you wrote, show your expression is still true when it returns.** A line or two each, grouped by module.
If a function cannot affect the expression, say so in one line. If it could, say which step keeps it true.
